title: Treasury Sanctions Former Democratic Republic of the Congo President for Ties to Armed Conflict
summary: The U.S. Treasury's OFAC sanctioned former DRC President Joseph Kabila for materially supporting M23 rebels and the Congo River Alliance (AFC), both U.S.-designated armed groups, as part of efforts to enforce the U.S.-brokered Washington Accords signed December 4, 2025. Kabila is accused of providing financial support to AFC, encouraging military defections, and seeking to install a candidate opposed to the current DRC government. The action targets continued instability in eastern DRC where M23 has captured major provincial capitals including Goma and Bukavu.
key_points: OFAC designated Joseph Kabila pursuant to Executive Order 13413, as amended by E.O. 13671, for materially assisting M23 and AFC
Kabila has provided financial support to AFC and encouraged FARDC troops to defect to AFC forces in eastern DRC
M23, backed by Rwanda (RDF sanctioned March 2, 2026), controls Goma and Bukavu—the capitals of North and South Kivu provinces
AFC leader Corneille Nangaa was originally sanctioned in 2019 and re-designated in July 2024
The sanctions support the December 4, 2025 Washington Accords for Peace and Prosperity brokered by the U.S.
All property and interests in property of designated persons in U.S. possession are blocked; entities 50% or more owned by blocked persons are also blocked
why_it_matters: This sanctions action reinforces the U.S.-brokered Washington Accords framework intended to stabilize eastern DRC and expand Regional Economic Integration covering trade, investment, and critical minerals supply chains. While not a traditional macro catalyst (rate decisions, GDP prints, Fed communications), it signals continued U.S. enforcement of sanctions on actors threatening regional stability—relevant for commodity markets given DRC's significance in cobalt and other critical minerals.
macro_context: The Washington Accords include commitments to 'enhance transparency in critical minerals supply chains,' which could affect global cobalt and battery material markets given DRC supplies a significant share of world's cobalt. However, this sanctions action alone does not directly change supply chains or market structures—it is enforcement of existing designations. The regional integration framework aims to expand trade and investment in the region.
